qs.q: Which medication acts as an anti-anginal therapy by directly reducing heart rate via action on the sinus node?
qs.e: Ivabradine reduces heart rate by direct action on the sinus node. While beta-blockers also slow heart rate, ivabradine specifically targets the sinus node directly as noted.

qs.q: What is the normal resting heart rate range for a healthy adult?
qs.e: Normal adult heart rate ranges from 60 to 100 bpm, with rates below 60 classified as bradycardia and above 100 as tachycardia. Values outside this range require careful clinical correlation.
qs.s: Vital Signs Assessment — Study Notes: MCQs

qs.q: Mr. Kamau, 54, had a cardiac transplant 6 months ago. His current blood pressure is 120/70 mmHg and heart rate is 100 bpm. Which of the following drugs would have the least effect on Mr. Kamau's heart rate?
qs.e: A transplanted heart is denervated (no sympathetic or parasympathetic innervation). It responds only to circulating catecholamines via direct receptor stimulation. Phenylephrine is a selective α1 agonist with no direct cardiac effects. Any heart rate changes would be indirect (reflex bradycardia from vasoconstriction), but reflexes are absent in denervated hearts.
qs.s: Basic Pharmacology - Study Guide — MCQ Bank

qs.q: What happens to the heart rate when a person receives a high dose of pure Alpha-1 agonist like Phenylephrine intravenously?
o: No change in the heart rate
qs.e: Phenylephrine causes intense vasoconstriction (inc BP), which triggers the baroreceptor reflex to slow the heart rate.
qs.s: Weekly Pharmacology Exam - April 21, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: Which receptor subtype is found in the heart and increases heart rate when stimulated?
qs.e: Beta-1 adrenergic receptors are primarily located in the heart and increase rate and contractility.

ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Heart rate is the number of times the heart beats per minute. It reflects the body's metabolic demand and is influenced by factors like age, activity, and health status. Deviations from the normal range can indicate underlying physiological or pathological processes.

sections.p: Heart rate is the number of ventricular contractions per minute, commonly measured by palpating a peripheral pulse or using an electrocardiogram (ECG). A normal resting heart rate for adults is typically between 60-100 beats per minute (bpm).
b: Count beats for 60 seconds or 30 seconds x 2.

sections.p: Physiological increases occur with exercise, stress, and fever. Pathological causes include dehydration, anemia, hyperthyroidism, sepsis, and cardiac arrhythmias. In infants, heart failure can present with a high heart rate.
b: Pathological: Sepsis, dehydration, anemia, hyperthyroidism, heart failure, arrhythmias.

sections.p: An elevated heart rate (tachycardia) may be asymptomatic or cause palpitations, shortness of breath, chest pain, dizziness, or syncope. A low heart rate (bradycardia) can lead to fatigue, dizziness, lightheadedness, and syncope.
b: Tachycardia: Palpitations, dyspnea, chest pain, syncope.

t.b: To assess rhythm, rate, and identify cardiac abnormalities. A regular sinus rhythm with a rate >100 bpm indicates sinus tachycardia. Irregular rhythms suggest other causes.
To detect anemia or infection. Anemia can cause compensatory tachycardia. Elevated white blood cell count suggests infection/sepsis.
To rule out hyperthyroidism. Elevated T3/T4 levels can cause tachycardia.
To check electrolytes and hydration status. Electrolyte imbalances or dehydration can affect heart rate.

sections.p: Sustained, very high heart rates can lead to reduced cardiac output, myocardial ischemia, heart failure, and syncope. In infants, a high heart rate with poor feeding and sweating suggests heart failure.
b: Chest pain or signs of myocardial ischemia.

sections.p: Management focuses on treating the underlying cause. For tachycardia, this may involve fluid resuscitation for dehydration, antibiotics for sepsis, or anti-thyroid medication. For bradycardia, pacing or atropine may be considered.
b: Treat underlying cause (e.g., fluids for dehydration, antibiotics for sepsis).
Rate control medications (e.g., beta-blockers) if indicated.

sections.p: Anxiety or panic attacks can mimic tachycardia. Fever can be mistaken for a primary cardiac issue. In infants, rapid breathing can be confused with a high heart rate.

A normal heart rate can be misleading in the presence of significant illness if the patient is on beta-blockers. Athletes may have a resting bradycardia that is physiological. Pain can increase heart rate, masking other signs.
b: Athletic conditioning can cause physiological bradycardia.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of very fast or very slow heart rate.
Heart rate accompanied by chest pain, shortness of breath, or fainting.
Heart rate in an infant with poor feeding, sweating, or rapid breathing.

faq.q: What is a normal heart rate for an adult?
faq.a: A normal resting heart rate for adults is typically between 60 and 100 beats per minute.

faq.q: What causes a fast heart rate (tachycardia)?
faq.a: Tachycardia can be caused by exercise, fever, stress, dehydration, anemia, hyperthyroidism, or certain medications.

faq.q: What causes a slow heart rate (bradycardia)?
faq.a: Bradycardia can be caused by certain medications, heart conditions, electrolyte imbalances, or can be a normal finding in well-conditioned athletes.
